title: Cross-Team Handoff Variation Pack
learningObjective: Shape a package that another team member could run safely, with Day 1 readiness controlled by current workflow definitions rather than old habits.
chapterConcept: Operational readiness, handoff clarity, and strongest-practice comparison
lifecycleCue: This pack assumes Discovery and Selection are already complete. The run focuses on Shaping, then review and iteration.
caseBrief: An onboarding team wants a reusable context envelope another coordinator can run without the original designer present. The package must prevent an old shortcut from making the employee look Day 1 ready before essential access is actually confirmed.
successCriteria: Keep instructions, evidence, dynamic facts, and checks visibly distinct.
Make precedence and missing-information handling explicit instead of implied.
Use a reviewable output contract that another reviewer could inspect quickly.
Make the package reliable enough to hand off without hidden assumptions.
outputReminder: Did the response follow the current source of record instead of weaker notes?
Did it keep the required format rather than collapsing into a generic paragraph?
Did it state uncertainty or escalation when facts were missing?

precedenceRules.label: Current readiness definition outranks old team habits and assumptions.
Manager assignment is enough to imply Day 1 readiness.

outputOptions.label: Readiness / What Is Missing / Handoff Note

handlingOptions.label: State the missing access step and route to the onboarding lead.
Ask for the missing access state before giving the readiness answer.
Assume access can be cleaned up after Day 1.

blocks.label: Workflow Handoff Writer
blocks.text: Act as a careful workflow handoff writer. Build a package another team can use without hidden assumptions or buried rules.

blocks.label: Use Only Approved Workflow Materials
blocks.text: Use only the approved onboarding workflow notes and current system-state details provided in this package. Do not fill gaps with generic onboarding advice.

blocks.label: Escalate When Access Evidence Is Missing
blocks.text: If the access state is incomplete or contradictory, say what is unknown and route the issue to the onboarding lead instead of guessing completion.

blocks.label: Approved Onboarding Flow
blocks.text: Approved onboarding sequence: confirm signed offer, create HR record, request system access, verify manager assignment, then send Day 1 readiness note.

blocks.label: Day 1 Readiness Definition
blocks.text: Current readiness definition: a Day 1 note can be sent only after HR record, manager assignment, and essential system access are all confirmed.

blocks.label: Old Team Habit
blocks.text: Old team habit: send the Day 1 note once the manager assignment appears, then clean up access later. This predates the current readiness definition.

blocks.label: Current Case Facts
blocks.text: Dynamic facts for this run: the offer is signed, the HR record is complete, the manager assignment is confirmed, but the essential analytics-system access ticket is still pending.

blocks.label: Cross-Team Handoff Request
blocks.text: Task: prepare the package another coordinator will use to answer whether the employee is Day 1 ready and what should happen next.

blocks.label: Handoff Output Contract
blocks.text: Output expectation: return sections titled Readiness, What Is Missing, and Handoff Note. Keep the language crisp and handoff-ready.

blocks.label: Readiness Integrity Check
blocks.text: Checks: if essential access is still pending, do not label the case Day 1 ready. Name the missing item and the routing action explicitly.

rationale.ROLE: Clarify that the package is for safe handoff, not just a one-off answer.
rationale.RULES: Set source limits and escalation behavior before the evidence and task appear.
rationale.REFERENCE: Keep the current readiness definition stronger than the old team habit.
rationale.DYNAMIC FACTS: Separate the current access gap from the stable workflow rules.
rationale.TASK: State the cross-team handoff job after the governing materials are visible.
rationale.OUTPUT: Use a durable, reviewable format that another coordinator can scan quickly.
rationale.CHECKS: Make the readiness stop-rule explicit so the model does not guess completion.

preferredPhrases: essential analytics-system access is still pending

exploreMore.prompt: Compare two envelopes that are both plausible: one prioritizes speed, the other prioritizes handoff safety. Which tradeoff is more reviewable?
exploreMore.focus: How output contract and checks support repeatable handoff use

branches.title: Speed-first version
branches.instruction: Collapse the output into one short handoff note and compare what becomes easier to miss.
branches.watchFor: Whether the missing access step stops being prominent.
branches.why: This shows why concise does not always mean reviewable.

branches.title: Safety-first version
branches.instruction: Keep the sectioned output and make the stop-rule explicit. Compare how easy it is for another person to continue the work.
branches.watchFor: Whether the missing step and route path stay obvious.
branches.why: This shows why handoff quality is a shaping decision, not just a content decision.

build: Keep the current readiness definition stronger than the old shortcut habit.
Shape the package so another coordinator could see the missing access step immediately.
Use the output contract and checks to make handoff quality visible.
copy: In the external run, watch whether the answer quietly treats manager assignment as enough for Day 1 readiness.
Check whether the output is still easy for another person to act on.
review: Did the answer block Day 1 readiness until essential access is confirmed?
Did it name the missing step and route path clearly?
Did the output stay in the requested handoff-ready format?
